title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
subtitle: Dissecting hydraulic steering, mechanical gears, DriveSys aluminium extrusions, and captive renewables

web_blocks.html: On a standalone basis, ZF Steering Gear (India) reports two primary segments. Auto Components (roughly 97% of standalone revenue and Renewable Energy (roughly 3%) [1][4]). Yet looking only at standalone accounts misses the biggest operational change of the last two years. In FY2026, standalone revenue stood at approximately ₹356.7 crore while consolidated revenue reached ₹571 crore (with total consolidated income near ₹598.9 crore [1][18]. That ~₹214 crore consolidated gap reflects the commercial ramp-up of wholly owned subsidiary DriveSys Systems Private Limited at Supa. This operates an aluminium extrusion and solar-frame division alongside backward-integrated machining [12][13].

web_blocks.takeaway: Consolidated revenue growth is now powered by two distinct engines: cyclical commercial-vehicle steering demand at the parent and industrial aluminium/solar-frame manufacturing at DriveSys.

web_blocks.html: To see how each unit actually makes money, it helps to walk through concrete, end-to-end commercial transactions across all four operating legs. The engineering requirements, customer economics, and margin structures differ sharply between heavy-duty hydraulics and commodity aluminium extrusion.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Example 1: Hydraulic Power Steering for a 35-Tonne M&HCV Tipper
web_blocks.subtitle: Core Auto Components Segment
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: When Tata Motors or Ashok Leyland builds a 35-tonne mining tipper or multi-axle haulage truck, front-axle loads exceed 7 tonnes. A driver cannot physically turn those front wheels at low speed using mechanical leverage alone without fatiguing or losing control.

Product & Engineering: The OEM specifies ZF Steering Gear's Ball & Nut Integral Hydraulic Power Steering Gear (3,75,000 units/year capacity across Shirur and Pithampur), paired with a hydraulic vane pump and steering column [2][20]. Inside the cast-iron housing—increasingly cast at Metacast Auto in Kolhapur [17]—recirculating steel balls convert steering-wheel rotation into linear piston force boosted by pressurized hydraulic oil.

Supply & Economics: The OEM qualifies the gear through multi-year durability testing and buys on a just-in-time schedule under zero-base costing contracts [8]. Because only ZF Steering Gear and ZF Rane Automotive hold production-scale validation in India [20], switching suppliers mid-platform is rare, giving the parent steady volume once a truck platform launches.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Example 2: Mechanical vs. Hydrostatic Steering on a 45-HP Farm Tractor
web_blocks.subtitle: Tractor & Legacy Mechanical Segment
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: Domestic tractor makers such as Mahindra, Force Motors, and regional farm-equipment OEMs sell into price-sensitive rural markets where smaller 30–40 HP tractors historically used manual steering to keep sticker prices low.

Product & Delivery: ZF Steering supplies Worm & Roller Mechanical Steering Gears (2,00,000 units/year capacity) for base tractor models. Meanwhile, higher-horsepower 45–60 HP tractors increasingly migrate to hydraulic power steering [2].

Economics & Structural Trend: Mechanical gears carry lower unit realizations than integral power steering units, so the industry shift toward power-assisted tractors acts as a natural value-per-vehicle upgrade. However, overall volumes remain tied to monsoon-driven farm sentiment [8].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Example 3: Anodised Aluminium Solar Frames from DriveSys (Supa)
web_blocks.subtitle: DriveSys Systems Private Limited
paragraphs: Customer & Problem: Indian solar photovoltaic module manufacturers scaling gigawatt-scale lines need corrosion-resistant, precision-mitred aluminium perimeter frames that meet domestic content requirements without relying on Chinese imports.

Product & Process: At Supa Parner Industrial Park, DriveSys melts aluminium into billets (27,000 MTPA), extrudes profiles through precision dies (20,000 MTPA), anodises them for weather resistance (9,600 MTPA), and machines them into 2.4 million solar frame sets per year [12].

Supply & Economics: Unlike bespoke truck steering gears, solar frames are conversion-margin industrial products where raw aluminium ingot prices pass through and profitability depends on press utilization, scrap control, and power efficiency. DriveSys's rapid ramp-up explains why consolidated sales jumped +16% in FY2026 and +53% YoY in Q2 FY2027 [1][12].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Example 4: Captive Wind & Grid-Tied Solar Generation
web_blocks.subtitle: Renewable Energy Segment
paragraphs: Operation: The company owns 8.10 MW of wind turbines in Satara, Ahmednagar, and Aurangabad (Maharashtra) and a 5.0 MW solar park in Charnka, Gujarat [4].

Economics: The Gujarat solar park sells power to GUVNL under a long-term PPA (historically ~₹7.94 crore annual revenue prior to tariff resets). Meanwhile, the Maharashtra wind turbines wheel electricity directly to the Vadu Budruk plant, covering roughly two-thirds of its power bill [4]. Because depreciation and maintenance are low once installed, this segment generates high-margin cash flow that buffers manufacturing downturns [10].

web_blocks.html: Putting these four examples together clarifies the investment tension. The legacy steering business enjoys high technical barriers and duopoly pricing structure, whereas DriveSys's aluminium and solar-frame business scales revenue rapidly but competes in a more commodity-like conversion market. Next, we examine how raw materials, OEM pricing rules, and working capital turn those sales into cash.

Geographically and end-market wise, ZF Steering Gear's consolidated revenue base now spans domestic M&HCVs, buses, tractors, aftermarket spares, renewable power generation. Utility-scale solar/industrial aluminium extrusions [1, 5, 6]. This diversification softens pure-play truck cyclicality. However, it also requires tracking two distinct industrial margin profiles—precision steel machining versus commodity-linked aluminium extrusion [5, 8].

In the renewable energy segment, wind and solar power generation assets (~3% of standalone revenue act primarily as an internal captive-power hedge and steady cash contributor rather than a growth driver [6]). By contrast, DriveSys Systems' ability to supply anodised aluminium solar frames and industrial extrusions ties the consolidated growth engine directly to India's domestic solar-module manufacturing expansion [5].
Aftermarket replacement kits—including seal kits, worm-and-sector repair sets, and remanufactured steering units—provide a high-margin cushion during OEM cyclical troughs [1, 4].
Each segment carries its own margin physics. Precision steering gears earn duopoly margins, while aluminium extrusions rely on high press utilisation.
Each segment runs on its own clock. Truck gears follow freight demand, while Supa frames track solar plant builds. Both need steady factory runs to earn cash.
Good plants win on steady shifts. Idle lines eat cash fast. Investors must watch plant mix closely.
Both business lines serve domestic industrial buyers directly. Truck steering requires tight tolerances and safety testing. Aluminium frames require high press speeds and low scrap rates.

epigraph.quote: A subsidiary that doubles consolidated revenue changes the economics of the entire enterprise, even when the parent company's name still points to the original product.
epigraph.author: Pass 1 Forensic Principle

book_paragraphs: If you only read the company's name, you would assume ZF Steering Gear makes nothing but truck steering boxes. On a standalone basis, that is almost true: roughly 97% of standalone revenue comes from automotive steering components, and the remaining 3% comes from wind and solar power. Yet when you look at the consolidated accounts for FY2026, a major gap jumps off the page. Standalone sales were about ₹356.7 crore, while consolidated sales reached ₹571 crore. That ₹214 crore difference comes from DriveSys Systems, a wholly owned subsidiary in Supa, Maharashtra, that has quietly become a second growth engine.

To make this concrete, picture four different commercial transactions inside the group. First, imagine Tata Motors or Ashok Leyland assembling a 35-tonne mining tipper. Because the front axle carries more than seven tonnes, a driver cannot turn the wheels safely by muscle alone. The truck maker buys a Ball and Nut Integral Hydraulic Power Steering unit from ZF Steering's Vadu Budruk or Pithampur plant, paired with a hydraulic pump and a cast-iron housing poured at its Kolhapur foundry, Metacast Auto. Once an OEM qualifies that steering gear on a truck platform, switching suppliers mid-cycle is rare.

Second, picture a 45-horsepower farm tractor sold into rural India. Entry-level tractors still use ZF Steering's simpler Worm and Roller mechanical gears, where the company has 2,00,000 units of annual capacity, while heavier tractors are upgrading to hydraulic power steering. That shift raises the rupee value the company earns per tractor, even when unit tractor sales grow slowly.

Third, step into the Supa plant of DriveSys Systems. Here, the company is not making steering gears at all—it is casting 27,000 tonnes of aluminium billets, extruding 20,000 tonnes of profiles, anodising them, and cutting up to 2.4 million aluminium solar-module frames a year for Indian solar panel makers. Those frames sell at high volumes on conversion margins, which explains why consolidated revenue surged +53% year-on-year in the September 2026 quarter.

Finally, picture the company's 8.10 MW of wind turbines in Maharashtra and 5 MW solar park in Gujarat. The wind turbines supply roughly two-thirds of the electricity needed by the flagship Pune plant, lowering factory power costs, while the Gujarat solar park sells electricity under a long-term state contract. Together, these four businesses give you a company with a sticky steering core, a fast-growing but lower-margin aluminium subsidiary, and a small renewable power cushion. Let us now trace how materials flow through those plants and how much cash survives at the bottom.
Keep both business engines—hydraulic truck steering and Supa aluminium extrusions—separate in your mental model, because their margins and customer cycles respond to different economic drivers.

book_subsections.title: Walking the Floor: Hydraulic Power Steering in Action
paragraphs: Let us make the core business concrete. Picture a 35-tonne tipper truck hauling iron ore out of an Odisha mine or a 12-metre intercity bus navigating a crowded highway interchange. Turning the front axle under twenty tonnes of load requires immense hydraulic force, delivered smoothly so the driver does not fight the wheel.

Inside the Shirur plant near Pune, ZF Steering Gear machines high-tensile steel worm shafts, piston racks, and cast-iron housings to micron-level tolerances. Paired with a vane-type hydraulic pump driven off the truck's engine and a precision bevel gear box, the assembly multiplies the driver's input torque while damping road shock.

Every time Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland, Mahindra, or VECV rolls a heavy truck off the line, that steering assembly is bolted directly onto the chassis [1, 4]. Because safety-critical steering failures trigger regulatory recalls, OEMs lock in dual-source or single-source awards years in advance, giving ZF Steering Gear and its chief rival ZF Rane roughly 90 percent of the domestic M&HCV steering market [10].

book_subsections.title: Inside DriveSys Systems and Metacast Auto
paragraphs: Now walk over to the second engine of the company: DriveSys Systems at Supa [5]. Here, the customer is no longer just a truck OEM. A domestic solar module manufacturer building utility-scale PV plants needs lightweight, corrosion-resistant anodised aluminium frames that can survive twenty-five years of monsoon rain and desert heat.

DriveSys melts aluminium into billets, extrudes them into custom structural profiles, and anodises them in-house to supply up to 2.4 million solar frame sets annually alongside industrial and EV structural extrusions [5]. That explains why consolidated sales jumped to ₹571 Cr in FY26 and ₹184 Cr in Q2 FY27 even when standalone truck steering grew at a steadier pace [8].

Meanwhile, backward-integrated subsidiary Metacast Auto in Kolhapur supplies precision SG-iron and grey-iron castings [11]. Controlling the foundry reduces external vendor bottlenecks on housings and brackets, though it also adds fixed-asset intensity to the consolidated balance sheet.

book_subsections.title: Why Segment Economics Differ Between Steel Steering and Aluminium Extrusion
paragraphs: You and I should never lump all revenue rupees together as if they carry the same quality. A rupee of hydraulic steering gear revenue comes from decades-old OEM homologation, custom tooling, and tight dimensional tolerances where switching costs are very high.

A rupee of aluminium extrusion and solar frame revenue from DriveSys Systems operates on different physics [5]. Aluminium billet casting and extrusion is fundamentally a conversion-spread and capacity-utilization business. Raw aluminium prices largely pass through, so profitability depends on keeping presses running full and maintaining anodising quality.

If DriveSys runs near full capacity on its 20,000 MTPA extrusion lines, it adds meaningful EBITDA dollars and diversifies the top line. If solar module customers squeeze conversion margins during an industry glut, however, DriveSys will always carry lower structural margins than core precision steering gears.

book_subsections.title: Following the Customer From Quarry Truck to Solar Farm
paragraphs: Think about how unusual it is for a single ₹709 Cr small-cap to serve two completely different parts of India's capital-expenditure cycle. In the morning, its Shirur plant ships hydraulic steering boxes to Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland for heavy highway haulers and mining tippers.

In the afternoon, its Supa subsidiary ships anodised aluminium perimeter frames to domestic solar panel assemblers scaling up under India's renewable energy push [5]. Both end-markets benefit from domestic infrastructure and manufacturing investment, yet their quarterly order rhythms are not identical.

That dual exposure helps explain why consolidated revenue accelerated even when traditional tractor and truck volumes grew at a more modest pace. As an investor, however, you must track both demand curves separately rather than treating ZF Steering Gear as a simple auto-only proxy.

book_subsections.title: The Aftermarket Cushion in Commercial Fleets
paragraphs: Indian commercial trucks often stay on the road for ten to fifteen years, logging hundreds of thousands of kilometres over rough highways. Long after the original factory warranty expires, fleet mechanics replace seals, bearings, and steering linkages.
Those replacement parts carry healthier margins than bulk OEM factory contracts and help keep the Shirur machining lines humming when new truck sales pause.

book_subsections.title: Evaluating Product Mix Resilience
paragraphs: A key advantage of serving both heavy commercial vehicles and agricultural tractors is that rural monsoon cycles and urban infrastructure cycles do not always peak or trough in the same year [1, 4]. When highway freight slows down, strong reservoir levels and rural tractor demand can cushion plant utilization at Shirur and Pithampur.

Adding DriveSys's solar module frames introduces a third demand driver tied to India's utility-scale renewable installations, further smoothing consolidated quarterly revenue across fiscal years [5, 8].

book_subsections.title: Balancing Precision Machining With High-Volume Extrusion
paragraphs: Inside a precision steering plant, value comes from micron-level tolerances, heat treatment, and multi-year OEM safety validation. A single heavy-duty steering gear carries high engineering content per kilogram of steel.

Inside an aluminium extrusion plant like DriveSys, value comes from throughput, billet quality, and keeping anodising tanks running around the clock. Understanding why those two margin profiles behave differently helps you avoid extrapolating one segment's economics onto the other.
